items.headline: Iran, GCC foreign ministers and Iraq to meet in Oman Monday in a bid to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz
items.detail: Iran's Foreign Ministry confirmed it will meet Gulf Cooperation Council foreign ministers and Iraq's counterpart in Oman on Monday, framed as an effort to 'promote better understanding among the countries of the region' after Iran and Oman spent weeks negotiating a temporary shipping lane, mine-clearing operation and short-term management plan for the Strait, through which roughly one-fifth of world oil supply normally flows. The Strait has been effectively disrupted since US-Israeli strikes on Iran began in late February, and Friday's news was the first concrete diplomatic signal markets have had in weeks: Brent pulled back from an intraday high above $109.97 to settle down 2.8% at $104.61, and WTI fell 2.4% to $100.05, even as both still posted 8-9% weekly gains. Desks should treat Monday's outcome, not any single data print, as the dominant catalyst for Asia's reopen -- options markets are already pricing a binary gap move, with a genuine de-escalation capable of unwinding a meaningful chunk of the premium built into crude since the conflict widened, while a disappointment would likely send oil straight back toward the $109-110 highs touched last week. The meeting's scope is limited to Hormuz specifically, so even a successful outcome would leave the separate, and currently worsening, Red Sea/Bab el-Mandeb front (see below) unresolved.
items.source: Al Jazeera, CBS News, CNBC, Reuters

items.headline: Houthi forces seize Yemen's Red Sea port of Mocha and reach the Hanish islands and Perim, opening a second maritime chokepoint risk
items.detail: Iran-aligned Houthi forces captured the Red Sea port city of Mocha after fierce fighting forced Yemeni government troops to retreat south toward Dhubab, then pushed on to seize the strategic Hanish archipelago and, by Friday, reached Perim island commanding the Bab el-Mandeb Strait itself -- the narrow chokepoint between Yemen and Djibouti that a large share of Suez-bound shipping and LNG cargoes must transit. This is described as the sharpest escalation along Yemen's western coast since a UN-brokered truce largely halted major hostilities in 2022, and it matters for markets because it opens a second potential shipping chokepoint distinct from, and geographically separate from, the Strait of Hormuz that Monday's Oman talks are meant to address. An estimated 20% of global LNG flows, mostly Qatari cargoes, are already being disrupted via Hormuz; a Houthi-controlled Bab el-Mandeb would threaten a second major artery simultaneously, which is a materially larger tail risk than either chokepoint alone. War-risk insurance, tanker rerouting costs and European gas prices (Dutch TTF already up 12% on the week per Friday's European session) are the most direct read-throughs, and this front is not covered by Monday's Hormuz-focused meeting, meaning it could keep a floor under crude even if the Oman talks succeed.
items.source: ABC News (Australia), CGTN, NewsCord, Business Standard

items.headline: DeepSeek's ultra-lean V4.1 Flash model is the real story behind Friday's Samsung/SK Hynix selloff, not just macro risk-off
items.detail: DeepSeek unveiled its V4.1 Flash model on September 10, priced as low as $0.15 per million tokens, built around an architecture that cuts key-value cache to just 890 bytes per token -- a quarter of its predecessor's HBM footprint and an eighth of its SSD writes. The announcement triggered a direct, identifiable sell-off: Samsung Electronics fell 3.5% and SK Hynix 2.2% in Seoul on Friday, while Micron and SK Hynix's US ADRs dropped more than 5% in New York, all clearly attributable to the model release rather than the oil/Treasury-yield backdrop that Friday's initial wire coverage emphasized for the Kospi's broader 1.76% decline. The debate splitting desks: bulls argue this is an architecture-specific KV-cache optimization rather than proof of a durable drop in aggregate HBM demand, since SK Hynix's and Samsung's already-committed capacity expansions could still run 12-24 months ahead of any generalized efficiency-driven demand slowdown; bears note that if rival labs replicate the technique, planned HBM capacity adds could meaningfully outrun realized demand. This is the key swing factor for whether Samsung, SK Hynix and the won stabilize or extend Friday's losses when Seoul reopens Monday.
items.source: Bloomberg, Seeking Alpha, ZeroHedge, BigGo Finance
items.time: model unveiled Sept 10, priced into Friday's Seoul close

items.headline: China's CSRC quietly rejects mandatory convertible bonds as a developer-restructuring tool, complicating Country Garden's $13bn plan
items.detail: The China Securities Regulatory Commission has declined to accept registration for a swathe of mandatory convertible bonds (MCBs), a debt-to-equity instrument that had become a key mechanism in major property developers' restructuring negotiations with foreign creditors. Country Garden -- partway through issuing up to $13bn of MCBs as part of restructuring $14.1bn of offshore debt in one of China's largest-ever corporate workouts -- was informed weeks ago that its own filing had been rejected on the grounds that it is a 'discredited entity' following prior defaults and regulatory violations. The move effectively removes, or at minimum weakens, one of the tools that had kept several major developers out of the liquidation that befell China Evergrande in 2024, and it lands the same week Bloomberg reported China Vanke was drawing up its own debt-restructuring plan at regulators' request after missing a quarterly interest payment. For Asia credit and distressed-debt desks, the read-through is that Beijing's tolerance for creative offshore-restructuring instruments may be narrowing even as it keeps nudging developers toward faster resolutions -- a dynamic that could resurface stress in China property-linked dollar credit that had otherwise been overshadowed this week by the equity-level AI/tech rally.

items.headline: TSMC's August sales jump 53.3% y/y as AI chip demand keeps outstripping supply; 2026 capex raised to $60-64bn
items.detail: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. reported August revenue of NT$514.8bn ($16.3bn), up 53.3% year-on-year and accelerating sharply from 36.0% growth in Q2 2026 and 20.4% in Q4 2025, prompting the company to raise full-year 2026 guidance to growth slightly above 40% in USD terms. TSMC also lifted its 2026 capital-expenditure budget to a range of $60-64bn and disclosed a cumulative $265bn planned investment in its Arizona fabs, underscoring how far the foundry/logic side of the AI buildout remains from any capacity ceiling. The news capped a week in which Semicon Taiwan, one of the world's largest chip trade shows, brought together TSMC, ASE, MediaTek, Unimicron and Foxconn -- Taiwan's so-called 'Five Tigers' -- on a joint panel discussing the island's AI ecosystem. The contrast with the DeepSeek-driven memory story above is the useful trade here: logic/foundry capacity looks structurally undersupplied even as fresh doubts emerge about memory demand, a bifurcation that single-name and sector-rotation desks running Asia semis exposure should track closely into next week.

items.headline: India's Sensex and Nifty extend to a fifth straight losing week as oil, Middle East risk and outflows compound
items.detail: India's Sensex closed Friday at 74,781.76, down 120.83 points, while the Nifty 50 ended at 23,398.10, down 79.25 points -- both benchmarks falling more than 2% for the week (Nifty roughly -2.7%, Sensex roughly -2.9%), extending their losing streak to five consecutive weeks. The drivers are the same complex hitting the rest of the region: rising crude is a direct terms-of-trade hit for oil-import-dependent India, escalating Middle East risk is keeping foreign investors defensive, and continued portfolio outflows are compounding the rupee's own slide toward record-low territory near 95.7-95.8/USD despite persistent RBI intervention. This is a genuinely multi-week trend rather than a single-day risk-off wobble, and EM Asia equity and FX desks should treat it as a structural derating in progress rather than noise -- with Monday's Oman-meeting outcome on Hormuz shipping as the next obvious swing factor for whether the losing streak extends to six.
items.source: India TV News, 5paisa, Business News This Week

items.headline: Chinese tech buybacks keep outrunning the Hang Seng Tech selloff -- Tencent's 2026 repurchases reach HK$49.95bn
items.detail: Tencent's cumulative share buybacks for 2026 reached HK$49.954bn as of September 11, equivalent to roughly 1.02% of its total share capital, part of a broader wave that also includes Alibaba's $4.1bn buyback program and repurchases from Meituan and Xiaomi, all aimed at shoring up investor confidence in Chinese mega-cap tech. Reporting flagged Tencent's own stock down a comparatively modest 1.8% this month against a roughly 10% slump in the Hang Seng Tech Index over the same window -- a divergence that argues large-cap buybacks are doing real, measurable work cushioning individual names against a sector-wide risk-off, rather than sentiment alone driving the gap. For desks running China-tech dispersion or benchmarking single names against the broader index, the buyback-versus-index gap is a live, quantifiable signal worth tracking alongside this week's other China storyline -- AI/cloud-linked equity strength (CSI Cloud Computing, CSI AI) sitting uneasily against renewed property-credit stress (see the Country Garden item above).
items.source: Bloomberg, South China Morning Post, Yahoo Finance

items.headline: China's August CPI holds at 0.8% y/y, PPI beats at 3.8% as factory-gate deflation continues to fade
items.detail: China's August CPI rose 0.8% year-on-year, up from July's six-month low of 0.5% and in line with consensus, with the month-on-month print at 0.4% versus 0.3% expected; core CPI (ex food and energy) climbed 1.0%, edging up from July's 0.9%. The producer price index rose 3.8% y/y, beating the 3.6% forecast and extending a rebound from a prolonged stretch of factory-gate deflation, with NBS statisticians citing volatile global commodity prices, seasonal food costs, and firmer high-tech, electronics and machinery demand. Neither print triggered a notable market reaction, but the PPI beat is an incremental positive for Chinese industrial margins and adds one more modest data point to the PBOC's calculus alongside the currency-fixing management story (yuan strength being deliberately slowed) flagged in Thursday and Friday's sessions.

items.headline: Bitcoin drifts back toward $77k after a failed Friday retest of $80k, a quiet crypto backdrop into FOMC week
items.detail: Bitcoin rallied to roughly $79,500-79,700 intraday Friday before the move was rejected, falling back into the $77,000-77,500 range heading into the weekend. With US spot ETFs closed and traditional-market catalysts absent on Saturday, price action looks set for a quieter consolidation phase barring crypto-native flow shocks. The failed retest is nonetheless a useful sentiment gauge for multi-asset and macro-fund desks treating crypto as a read on speculative risk appetite heading into a week stacked with event risk -- the FOMC on September 16, the BOJ on September 18, and Monday's binary Oman-meeting outcome -- a lot for a market that couldn't hold a bounce even before any of it lands.

items.headline: Gold holds a quiet $4,350-4,365 range as the dollar/safe-haven tug-of-war persists into the weekend
items.detail: Spot gold trades around $4,348-4,362/oz in early Saturday quotes, essentially a continuation of the $4,365-4,410 band that has held since midweek and modestly softer than Friday's roughly $4,385 late reading. The metal remains caught between a firmer dollar on elevated Fed-hike odds into next week's FOMC and safe-haven demand from an unresolved, and in places widening, Middle East conflict. Gold is still roughly 22% below its January 2026 record above $5,589, even as global ETF inflows ran at a near-record $17.9bn in August, underscoring that the structural institutional bid remains intact beneath the currently rangebound spot price. Monday's Oman-meeting outcome and next week's FOMC/BOJ decisions are the likeliest catalysts to finally break the range.
items.source: JM Bullion, World Gold Council, USAGold

items.headline: Copper holds near $6.46-6.47/lb as Chinese buyers use the pullback to restock inventory
items.detail: Copper trades around $6.46-6.47/lb, essentially flat over the past session and continuing a mild pullback from its highs, but still up roughly 41% over the trailing year on structural AI/data-center-linked demand growth. With Chinese buyers representing an estimated 60% of global copper demand, reporting points to buyers using the lower prices to replenish inventories rather than to fund a construction recovery -- grids and EVs, not property, remain the dominant Chinese demand driver. The metal's resilience even amid this week's broader equity risk-off reinforces copper's ongoing decoupling from the property-driven China growth narrative in favor of the electrification/AI-buildout one.
items.source: Trading Economics, Rio Times, IEA commentary

items.headline: Iron ore holds near $99-100/tonne even as Chinese crude steel output falls to its weakest July since 2017
items.detail: The 62%-Fe benchmark delivered into China has held near a nine-week high around $99.57/tonne after touching just under $100 in early September, even though China's crude steel output fell 3.6% y/y to 76.93mt in July -- the weakest July reading since 2017. The apparent contradiction resolves once imports are considered: China imported 736.84mt of iron ore in the first seven months of 2026, up 6% y/y, but mills appear to be restocking to rebuild inventory buffers rather than to feed a construction recovery, meaning the current price floor is cost- and freight-driven rather than demand-driven. For Australian mining-equity exposure (BHP, Rio Tinto, Fortescue all have direct read-through via the ASX 200), the setup argues the price band is more fragile than it looks, with a decisive break above $100 requiring an actual improvement in Chinese downstream demand rather than just restocking flow.

items.headline: ECB delivers a hawkish 25bp hike to 2.50%, its second of the year, as Iran-war energy inflation forces policy back into tightening mode
items.detail: The European Central Bank raised its deposit rate a quarter point to 2.50% (main refi to 2.65%) on Thursday, the second hike since the US-Israeli war on Iran began reshaping the energy-price backdrop, after euro-area headline inflation accelerated to 3.3% y/y in August -- its highest since September 2023 -- with energy inflation alone running near 14.3%. President Lagarde called the move a 'no-brainer' and delivered a markedly more hawkish tone than the hike itself implied, explicitly declining to rule out an October follow-up; markets responded by pricing roughly a 90% chance of a third hike this year and a deposit rate near 2.70-2.75% by December. Crucially, the ECB simultaneously lifted its growth projections for this year and next, judging the euro-area economy resilient enough to absorb the energy shock without recession, while keeping its inflation forecast above the 2% target through 2027 on a €82/MWh gas-price assumption. This is the textbook 3-star, cross-asset event: it repriced the entire euro rates curve, split equities along rate-sensitivity lines (banks up, long-duration tech down), pushed Bund yields to multi-year highs, and is the reason STOXX 600 fell to a two-month low on the announcement before partially recovering Friday. Desks should treat Monday's Iran-GCC talks in Oman on Hormuz shipping (see Asia panel) as the next swing factor for whether the ECB's tightening path steepens further or the energy-inflation premise starts to unwind.
items.source: Bloomberg, CNBC, Reuters (via Yahoo Finance), Rio Times Europe Intelligence Brief
items.time: decision 14:15 CET Thursday Sept 10; repriced through Friday's session

items.headline: German Bund 10-year yield presses toward its highest since 2011 as ECB tightening bets build
items.detail: The German 10-year Bund yield has pushed up toward roughly 3.4-3.45%, a level not seen since 2011, as Thursday's ECB hike and Lagarde's hawkish commentary reinforced expectations for at least one more move this year. The move reflects a straightforward repricing mechanism: with the ECB's own forecasts keeping inflation above target through 2027, the market is demanding materially more term premium across the curve, and the sell-off has been broad-based across German, French and peripheral government debt. For rates desks, the level matters less than the trajectory -- a 3.4%+ Bund with the ECB still explicitly leaving the door open to October action reduces the odds of a near-term consolidation in European duration, and increases the odds that credit spread widening (high-yield and subordinated bank debt in particular) becomes the next transmission channel if growth data disappoints even slightly.

items.headline: UK 10-year gilt yield hits its highest since August 2007 at 5.295% as BoE hike bets compound with the ECB move
items.detail: The UK 10-year gilt yield struck 5.295% on Thursday, the highest print since August 2007, extending a UK-specific bond sell-off that predates but has now been amplified by the ECB's hawkish hike. Stronger-than-expected UK GDP data released Friday added to the case for further Bank of England tightening, with sterling stabilizing near $1.352 (GBP/USD +0.06%) as traders digested both the domestic growth beat and the region-wide rates repricing. The UK 30-year gilt yield has meanwhile held around 5.93%, underscoring that the move is a genuine curve-wide phenomenon rather than a front-end-only story. This is a clear, tradable single-asset-class move (>5bp, multi-day) that matters beyond gilts specifically -- UK mortgage and corporate borrowing costs, and by extension UK housing and credit-sensitive equities, all reprice off this benchmark, and the level is now firmly in territory last associated with the 2007-08 pre-crisis period.
items.source: Global Banking & Finance, Trading Economics, FX.co
items.time: yield struck 09:30 GMT Thursday; GDP data and sterling reaction Friday

items.headline: French OAT-Bund spread grinds toward 85bp as fiscal and political risk keeps a premium on French debt
items.detail: France's 10-year OAT yield has climbed to roughly 4.31%, its highest in around 14 years, pushing the OAT/Bund spread out to about 85 basis points as of early September -- up sharply from roughly 55bp at the start of the year. The move is being driven by investor skepticism that Paris can deliver material fiscal consolidation given the political backdrop, with markets openly discussing scenarios around a possible change of government or policy priorities next year and a 2026 debt-service bill approaching €65bn, now the state's single largest budget line. Layered on top of the ECB's hawkish pivot, French sovereign risk is the periphery-adjacent story euro rates and credit desks are watching most closely -- a spread that was tight and stable earlier in the year is now trending wider on a slope that, if it continues, starts to bleed into French bank funding costs and OAT-linked derivatives positioning.
items.source: CNBC, Ideal-Investisseur, Amundi Research Center, Cointribune
items.time: spread as of early September, trending into this week

items.headline: STOXX 600 rebounds 0.3% Friday to 637.60 but still on track for its worst week since April after Thursday's ECB-driven two-month low
items.detail: The pan-European STOXX 600 fell to a two-month low on Thursday (roughly -0.5%) as the ECB's hawkish hike hit rate-sensitive names, then recovered 0.3% to 637.60 on Friday as investors reassessed the growth-upgrade half of the ECB's message. Even with Friday's bounce, the index is on course for its steepest weekly decline since April, as elevated bond yields and lingering worry about further hikes offset otherwise resilient earnings momentum heading into key US CPI data later Friday. The pattern -- a policy-driven air pocket followed by a partial, unconvincing recovery -- is the signature of a market still working out whether the ECB's hawkish tone or its growth upgrade is the more important signal, and leaves the index vulnerable to a retest of the Thursday lows if Monday's Hormuz talks in Oman disappoint or US CPI surprises to the upside.

items.headline: DAX closes Friday +0.82% at 25,569 but the tape splits sharply: Infineon and Siemens lead, Rheinmetall and BASF lag
items.detail: Germany's DAX added 207 points (+0.82%) to close at 25,569 on Friday, but the composition of the move is more informative than the headline: Infineon (+4.78%), Siemens (+2.73%) and Deutsche Telekom (+2.55%) led, while Rheinmetall (-3.05%), BASF (-2.83%) and Henkel (-1.71%) were the weakest performers. Rheinmetall's slide extends a pullback that began after JPMorgan placed the stock on a Negative Catalyst Watch earlier in the week, even as the company continues to report strong order momentum (including a fresh US Marine Corps unmanned-ground-vehicle order) -- a case of positioning and valuation risk outweighing fundamentals for now. BASF's weakness is consistent with the broader energy-cost squeeze German chemicals face as gas prices push toward 2023 highs on the Iran-war LNG disruption (see below), while Infineon and Siemens' gains suggest capex-cycle and AI-infrastructure exposure is still finding buyers even in a rate-hostile tape. For single-name and sector-rotation desks, this dispersion -- not the index headline -- is the more durable signal out of Frankfurt today.

items.headline: European bank stocks outperform post-ECB as higher rates flow straight to net interest margin: Santander, SocGen, Deutsche Bank all higher
items.detail: Banking stocks were the clearest beneficiaries of Thursday's ECB hike, with Banco Santander adding roughly 0.7%, Societe Generale gaining around 1.6%, and Deutsche Bank rising 1.3%, even as the broader STOXX 600 fell to a two-month low the same session. Santander's strength is being reinforced by a sizeable ongoing share buyback and, separately, by the EU's clearance of its Ebury cross-border payments deal, giving the stock a company-specific tailwind layered on top of the sector-wide rate story. The mechanism is straightforward and well understood by desks: a steeper, higher policy rate path widens net interest margin for European lenders faster than it raises their funding or credit-loss costs in the near term, which is why bank equities have decoupled positively from the broader index even as rate-sensitive growth and tech names (SAP, ASML) sold off in the same session. This dispersion is a clean, tradable expression of the ECB story for anyone running European financials versus the broader index.
items.time: Thursday's ECB-decision session, extending into Friday

items.headline: SAP extends its slide toward multi-month lows as a trimmed profit outlook and a Santander downgrade overshadow strong cloud growth
items.detail: SAP shares fell a further 2.8% to €177.82 on Thursday, roughly 24% below their 52-week high of €242 set last October, as the stock absorbed both a Santander downgrade and lingering digestion of a trimmed full-year non-IFRS operating profit guidance range of €11.8-12.2bn. The disconnect is notable: SAP's Current Cloud Backlog rose 26% currency-adjusted to €22.9bn last quarter with cloud revenue up 24%, yet the market is choosing to price the guidance trim and valuation concerns over the underlying growth story, a pattern reinforced by a cluster of freshly published security notes that added to sentiment pressure. Combined with ASML's roughly 1.1% decline in the same ECB-hike session, SAP's weakness underlines how European rate-sensitive, long-duration tech names are bearing a disproportionate share of the pain from the hawkish repricing even as the broader software/cloud fundamentals hold up -- a valuation-versus-fundamentals split worth tracking into next week's price action.

items.headline: Dutch TTF gas pushes toward €73-74/MWh, its highest since early 2023, as the Iran war chokes LNG flows into a critical restocking window
items.detail: The Dutch TTF benchmark, Europe's reference gas price, has climbed to roughly €73-74/MWh, a level last seen in early 2023, as the ongoing US-Israeli war on Iran keeps the Strait of Hormuz -- which normally carries about a fifth of global LNG trade -- effectively shut, and the Houthi advance to Bab el-Mandeb (flagged in the Asia panel) raises the prospect of a second chokepoint. The timing is unusually painful: European utilities are in the middle of their pre-winter storage-refill season, meaning any sustained LNG shortfall shows up directly in spot gas prices rather than being smoothed by inventory buffers. This is the direct commodity-market read-through of the same Iran-war narrative driving the ECB's inflation forecasts (the central bank's own projections assume €82/MWh gas), and it is the mechanism linking the geopolitical story in the Middle East to European household heating bills, industrial input costs (see BASF above) and, ultimately, the ECB's reaction function into October.

items.headline: Turkish lira grinds to a fresh record low near 48.5/USD as the central bank holds its policy rate at 37% for a fifth straight meeting
items.detail: The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey (CBRT) held its benchmark rate at 37% for a fifth consecutive decision, in line with expectations, even as it acknowledged that surging energy prices tied to the Iran-US war are adding fresh inflationary risk on top of an underlying disinflation trend the bank says has continued since June. The lira nonetheless slipped to a fresh record low near 48.5 per dollar, consistent with the CBRT's policy of continuing to manage a slow, controlled devaluation rather than defending a hard level, while policymakers downplayed any imminent return to the one-week repo auctions suspended since March -- keeping banks reliant on the more expensive overnight facility. For EM and CEEMEA FX desks, the read is that Turkey's currency-management framework remains intact and the market has grown largely desensitized to the headline devaluation pace, but the Iran-war energy channel is now a live upside risk to the CBRT's own disinflation narrative that bears watching alongside the broader European energy story.
items.source: Trading Economics, ING THINK CEEMEA FX Outlook
items.time: CBRT decision this week; lira weakness ongoing into Friday

items.headline: Tata Motors' €3.8bn tender offer for Iveco clears its final hurdle, tender window runs to October 26
items.detail: Tata Motors' acceptance window for its €3.8bn (€14.10/share cash) tender offer for Italy's Iveco Group opened September 7 and runs through October 26, after Italy's Consob cleared the offer on September 3 following ECB approval on September 1 -- the last major regulatory box left to tick. The deal creates a combined global commercial-vehicle group with roughly €22bn in annual revenue spanning Europe, Asia and Latin America, and settlement for accepting shareholders is pencilled in for October 30 (with a possible reopened window in early November). It is a straightforward large-cap corporate-action story for European autos/industrials desks to track through the acceptance period rather than a fresh catalyst today, but worth flagging given the size and the read-through for European truck-sector consolidation.

items.headline: Gold ticks up toward $4,348-4,362/oz as the ECB hike and a firm dollar offset safe-haven demand
items.detail: Spot gold gained roughly 0.8% to around $4,348/oz, a continuation of the choppy $4,350-4,410 range that has held through the week, as a firmer dollar into next week's FOMC and the ECB's own hawkish hike offset the safe-haven bid that would otherwise come from an unresolved Middle East conflict. The metal remains well below its January 2026 record above $5,589, even as institutional demand (per the Asia panel, near-record August ETF inflows) stays structurally supportive underneath the range. Nothing here breaks the pattern flagged in the Asia session -- gold is waiting on Monday's Oman talks and next week's FOMC/BOJ decisions to pick a direction.

items.headline: EUR/USD softens toward $1.16 and GBP/USD firms to $1.352 as the dollar holds a bid ahead of US CPI
items.detail: The euro slipped modestly toward $1.16 on Friday even after the ECB's hawkish hike, as the dollar stayed broadly supported ahead of the US CPI print due later in the session -- a reminder that Fed-versus-ECB path expectations, not the ECB decision alone, are driving the pair near-term. Sterling, by contrast, firmed to around $1.352 (+0.06%) on the back of stronger-than-expected UK GDP data and the accompanying lift in gilt yields and BoE hike bets, while EUR/GBP has struggled to clear resistance near 0.8600. None of this is a fresh directional break, but the divergence between a soft euro and a firm pound on the same day both central banks are in tightening mode is a useful cross-currency signal for G10 FX desks running EUR/GBP or relative-rate trades into next week.

items.headline: SNB seen holding at 0% on September 25 despite August inflation doubling and strong Swiss growth
items.detail: Economists surveyed by Reuters expect the Swiss National Bank to hold its policy rate at 0% at its September 25 meeting and through the rest of 2026, even though Swiss inflation doubled in August and quarterly growth hit its fastest pace in nearly five years -- a combination that would typically raise hike odds. The franc has traded near $0.81, its softest since August 19, and the SNB has signaled greater readiness to intervene in FX markets if needed, with Middle East-driven safe-haven flows a wildcard that could still push the franc stronger regardless of the rate decision. This is pure context for now -- no near-term SNB move is priced -- but it is one more data point on how differently European central banks are responding to the same energy-inflation shock the ECB and BoE are actively fighting.

items.headline: Eurozone Q2 GDP confirmed at +0.6% q/q, underpinning the ECB's decision to raise growth forecasts alongside Thursday's hike
items.detail: Eurostat's second read confirmed euro-area GDP grew 0.6% q/q in Q2 2026 (1.0% y/y), with industrial production data through the summer also holding up better than feared given the scale of the energy shock from the Iran war. This resilience is precisely why the ECB felt able to hike rates while simultaneously lifting its growth projections on Thursday -- the central bank's message is that the euro-area economy can absorb higher energy costs and higher rates at the same time, at least for now. It's an in-line, no-surprise data point with no standalone market reaction, but it is the macro underpinning for this week's entire ECB-hawkish-hike narrative and worth holding in mind against next week's incoming data.
items.time: released this week, referenced in Thursday's ECB projections
